cards.headline: Trump, Vance to headline GOP midterm convention alongside vulnerable candidates
cards.teaser: A preliminary speaker list shows the president and vice president appearing with Senate and House Republicans in competitive races, while Senate Majority Leader John Thune is notably absent.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump and his top allies will share the stage with Republican candidates in some of the nation's most competitive races at next week's GOP midterm convention in Dallas, according to a preliminary list of speakers. Trump will speak both nights of the September 9-10 convention, while Vice President JD Vance will deliver a keynote address on the second night. The lineup also includes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Donald Trump Jr.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who Trump has attacked for not doing more to pass election security legislation, is notably absent from the list, though organizers say they are still adding names. Republicans in some of the toughest races are not attending, including Senator Susan Collins in Maine and former Senator John Sununu in New Hampshire. Senate candidates scheduled to appear include Ohio Senator Jon Husted, Texas Republican Ken Paxton, and Michigan Republican Mike Rogers. About 100 Republican lawmakers and candidates are expected to attend the convention.

cards.headline: Trump envoys meet with Putin in Moscow, plan Ukraine trip amid airstrike pause
cards.teaser: President Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday and discussed U.S. ideas for ending the war in Ukraine.
cards.body:
President Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday and discussed U.S. ideas for ending the war in Ukraine. The three-hour meeting came as both countries agreed to a short pause in airstrikes to allow the envoys to travel to Kyiv on Sunday.

Putin told Witkoff and Kushner at the start of the meeting that he has full trust in U.S. mediation between Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman and for agreeing to pause airstrikes against Ukraine while U.S. negotiators visit Kyiv. Putin said the pause will begin at midnight Saturday Moscow time and noted that Ukraine also reduced its strikes.

The envoys are seeking to resume direct talks between Russia and Ukraine after negotiations were suspended six months ago and fighting has escalated ahead of winter. Over the last several days, Russia dramatically increased its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine, including Kyiv and other major cities.

The trip to Kyiv will be the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to Ukraine since President Trump started his second term. If the U.S. government plane carrying Witkoff and Kushner lands in Ukraine on Sunday, it will be the first international flight to land in the country since the war started in February 2022.

cards.headline: Trump plans to use Qatari plane for Ireland trip despite security concerns

cards.body:
President Donald Trump will fly to Ireland next week aboard a Boeing 747 gifted by Qatar, despite ongoing security concerns about the aircraft. Plans to take the plane out of service for security upgrades have been pushed back to later this fall.

The decision to use the Qatari-gifted aircraft for international travel raises questions about the readiness of the plane for presidential use. Security upgrades that officials had planned to implement before the aircraft entered regular service will now be delayed until after the Ireland visit.

The Boeing 747 was a gift from Qatar to the United States. Presidential aircraft typically undergo extensive modifications and security enhancements before being cleared for use in transporting the president on foreign trips. The standard security protocols for presidential travel include advanced communications systems, defensive countermeasures, and other classified protections.

The Ireland trip marks one of Trump's first major international visits since the escalation of tensions in the Middle East, including the ongoing conflict with Iran that has affected oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz. The decision to proceed with the trip using the unupgraded aircraft suggests the White House views the security measures currently in place as sufficient for the journey.

The postponement of security upgrades until later this fall means the aircraft will continue flying in its current configuration for at least several more weeks. Officials have not disclosed what specific security enhancements are planned or why the upgrades could not be completed before the international trip.

cards.headline: Supreme Court rules political parties entitled to lower TV ad rates
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court delivered a significant victory to Republican and Democratic party organizations Friday, ruling that political parties are entitled to discounted television adver
cards.body:
The Supreme Court delivered a significant victory to Republican and Democratic party organizations Friday, ruling that political parties are entitled to discounted television advertising rates when they coordinate spending with candidates.

The decision addresses a long-standing dispute over how broadcast stations must price political advertising under federal communications law. Broadcasters are required to offer candidates the lowest unit rate for ad time during the weeks before an election, but questions have persisted about whether this rule applies to party committees that coordinate with campaigns. The court's ruling extends these discounted rates to party organizations, potentially saving national and state party committees millions of dollars in advertising costs.

The timing of the decision comes as both major parties prepare for the 2026 midterm elections in November, when control of Congress and numerous state offices will be decided. Political advertising spending for the 2026 cycle is expected to reach record levels, with television continuing to serve as a dominant medium even as digital platforms grow in importance. Party committees, which are permitted to raise larger contributions than individual candidates under federal law, play a crucial role in funding competitive races across the country.

The ruling could substantially reshape the financial landscape of campaign advertising by making party-funded television spots significantly less expensive during the critical final weeks leading up to elections. Television stations had opposed the extension, arguing that providing lowest unit rates to coordinated party spending would reduce their advertising revenue and create administrative difficulties. Campaign finance reform advocates have raised concerns that the decision could strengthen the influence of party organizations over individual candidates.

The Supreme Court has not yet released the complete opinion or provided details about the vote breakdown. Legal experts anticipate that the ruling will encourage parties to shift more resources toward traditional broadcast advertising in competitive markets, particularly in swing states and districts where television can reach large numbers of voters who might be persuadable.

The decision addresses a fundamental question about how federal communications law applies to party spending when it is coordinated with candidates. Broadcasters maintain strict pricing rules designed to ensure that candidates have access to affordable advertising, but the precise scope of these requirements has been contested when party organizations make related purchases.

Political parties have long sought equal treatment with candidates under advertising rate regulations. The court's decision validates their argument that coordinated party spending should qualify for the same favorable pricing that candidates receive. This ruling could accelerate a significant shift in how campaign funds are allocated and spent, with parties potentially redirecting resources from other activities to maximize their television advertising capacity during crucial election periods.

cards.headline: Congress delays government funding and Iran war money until after midterms
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers have voted to postpone major legislative decisions until after the November midterm elections, setting up a crowded agenda for the final weeks of the year. The
cards.body:
Republican lawmakers have voted to postpone major legislative decisions until after the November midterm elections, setting up a crowded agenda for the final weeks of the year. The House overwhelmingly passed a bill to temporarily fund the government, pushing the deadline past Election Day and into the lame-duck session.

The postponed items include government funding, additional money for the ongoing conflict with Iran, and the extension of expanded surveillance authorities. GOP leaders chose to avoid these potentially divisive votes in the weeks leading up to the election, when control of the House hangs in the balance.

The decision creates a compressed timeline between the election and the Christmas recess, when lawmakers will need to address multiple high-stakes issues simultaneously. The lame-duck period, when some members will have already lost their seats or be preparing to leave office, typically makes legislative negotiations more challenging.

The strategy reflects the political sensitivity of these issues in an election year. Government funding debates often lead to shutdown threats, while votes on war spending and surveillance powers can divide both parties. By postponing these votes, Republican leadership aims to avoid giving Democratic challengers ammunition in competitive races.

The Iran war funding has become increasingly urgent as the conflict escalates. The U.S. has launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counter strikes by Tehran targeting American interests in multiple locations in the Middle East, including intense ballistic missile attacks on U.S. bases. President Trump warned after Tuesday's U.S. strikes that any Iranian retaliation would be met with responses at "a much harder and higher level."

The escalating exchange of attacks has intensified concerns about a wider renewal of hostilities in the region. Russia's Vladimir Putin has signaled unwavering support for Iran, with Tehran thanking Moscow for backing amid the escalating Middle East war.

The surveillance authorities in question are set to expire, and their extension has drawn opposition from privacy advocates within both parties. Congressional leaders will need to navigate these competing pressures in a shortened timeframe after voters have already rendered their verdict on the current Congress.

The bloated lame-duck agenda will be difficult to complete by Christmas, according to congressional observers. The decision to delay these major decisions reflects the political calculations of Republican leadership heading into the midterm elections, but creates significant challenges for legislative action once the election results are determined.

cards.headline: Whistleblower warns rushed USPS portal could reject ballots before midterms
cards.teaser: A federal official has warned that a hastily implemented U.S. Postal Service online system connected to President Trump's mail voting order could reject large batches of ballots ah
cards.body:
A federal official has warned that a hastily implemented U.S. Postal Service online system connected to President Trump's mail voting order could reject large batches of ballots ahead of the midterm elections. The whistleblower claims the USPS is rolling out the portal without sufficient testing or safeguards, creating concerns about potential disruptions to voting access.

The online system is being developed in response to Trump's efforts to restrict mail voting. According to the whistleblower, the accelerated timeline could result in technical failures that prevent eligible voters from receiving or submitting their ballots. The official stated that the implementation could potentially "derail" the midterm election if courts allow the plan to move forward.

The USPS portal would represent a significant change to how mail-in voting is processed. The system's design and operational readiness have become central concerns as the midterm elections approach. The whistleblower's allegations indicate that the agency is prioritizing speed over reliability in launching the new technology.

The warning emerges as courts consider challenges to Trump's mail voting restrictions. If legal challenges are unsuccessful and the portal proceeds as planned, election administrators could encounter unprecedented complications when processing absentee ballots. The potential for widespread ballot rejections raises important questions about voter access and election integrity.

Election officials, voting rights advocates, and lawmakers will likely examine the USPS implementation plans closely in the coming weeks. The outcome could affect millions of voters who depend on mail-in ballots, particularly in states with substantial absentee voting populations.

The situation highlights broader concerns about the implementation of voting systems and the importance of adequate testing before launch. Election experts generally emphasize that new voting infrastructure requires extensive preparation and validation to ensure it functions reliably when it matters most.

The USPS has not publicly responded to the whistleblower's claims. The agency typically coordinates with state election officials on mail delivery matters, and any changes to voting procedures would likely require coordination across multiple jurisdictions.

Election administrators in various states have expressed interest in understanding the details of any new USPS procedures. States manage their own voting systems, and changes at the federal level could create complications if they are not clearly communicated and tested beforehand.

The controversy adds uncertainty to the upcoming midterms at a time when election officials are already managing complex logistics. The potential technical issues identified by the whistleblower underscore the need for thorough testing and clear communication between federal agencies and state election officials before new systems go live.
